explanations.explanation: Paul says, "We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have exploited no one." Three "no one"s in a row, friend. That's a man reading off a clean list. And he says it while asking for room in their hearts.

The text says the opposite. Paul writes, "We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have exploited no one." That's three "no one"s lined up like cookies on a tray. So he says his team has wronged nobody.

explanations.answer: So close they live and die together
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "…you so occupy our hearts that we live and die together with you." That's not a casual friendship, friend. That's moving-in-and-staying closeness. And he says it right after making clear he isn't condemning them.

explanations.answer: Like trusted partners in the work
explanations.explanation: Partners are great, but that's not the picture Paul paints here. He says, "…you so occupy our hearts that we live and die together with you." Partners can clock out at five. Paul talks about living and dying together.

explanations.answer: Like guests who are always welcome
explanations.explanation: A guest comes, a guest goes, and somebody washes the extra dishes. Paul goes deeper than that. He says, "…you so occupy our hearts that we live and die together with you." Nobody is just visiting.

Paul says the opposite. He writes, "I am filled with encouragement; in all our troubles my joy overflows." Overflows, friend, not runs dry. That's a mixing bowl with the dough climbing over the sides.

Paul says, "…in all our troubles my joy overflows." The troubles are real, and the joy is bigger. His confidence and pride are great, and he says he's filled with encouragement too. His joy doesn't run dry.

Paul says they were pressed from every direction, with "conflicts on the outside, fears within." Trouble was coming at them from both sides. I think that's about the most tiring way to be squeezed. And it sets up what comes next.
Those two don't show up in this verse. Paul says "conflicts on the outside, fears within." It's easy to grab words that sound like they fit. Stay with what he actually wrote.

Prisons and grief aren't what Paul lists here. He says they were pressed with "conflicts on the outside, fears within." Same squeezed feeling, different list, friend. Check the verse and you'll find it.

Paul writes that "God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus." Titus worked alongside Paul. Notice who gets the credit. God is the one doing the comforting, and Titus is how it arrived.

Timothy, a fellow worker of Paul's (Romans 16:21), is a good name to know. But he's not the one in this verse. Paul says God comforted them "by the arrival of Titus." Two T names, friend. Easy to mix up.

Barnabas, set apart with Paul for God's work (Acts 13:2), doesn't show up in this verse. The comfort came by the arrival of Titus. Paul says it plainly: "But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus." I've got a whole pantry of names too, and I still grab the wrong one sometimes.

explanations.answer: Their longing and zeal for Paul
explanations.explanation: Paul says Titus "told us about your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me…" Good news, delivered in person. Notice the zeal is for Paul. That's why he says he rejoiced all the more.
Complaints would have been a heavy report. But Paul says Titus "told us about your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me…" That's a very different message. And it made Paul rejoice.

explanations.answer: Their plans to stop writing Paul
explanations.explanation: Paul never mentions anything like that. He says Titus "told us about your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me…" Longing means they wanted him close. Nobody was hanging up the phone.

Paul says Titus told them about the Corinthians' longing, mourning and zeal, "so that I rejoiced all the more." All the more, friend. He was already comforted, and then the joy piled on top. That's a cookie jar that gets refilled.
Titus's news brought the opposite. Paul says, "so that I rejoiced all the more." The worry in Macedonia was real, but this report didn't add to it. It lifted it.
No hesitating here. Paul says the news came "so that I rejoiced all the more." He's not standing at the oven door wondering whether to open it. He's celebrating.
Paul writes, "Even if I caused you sorrow by my letter, I do not regret it." He owns that it hurt. He doesn't pretend it didn't. And he stands by sending it.

explanations.answer: He wants them to forget it
explanations.explanation: Paul never asks them to forget anything. He says, "Even if I caused you sorrow by my letter, I do not regret it." You don't ask somebody to forget a thing you stand behind. He talks about it right out loud.

explanations.answer: He plans to take it back
explanations.explanation: No taking back here. Paul says, "Even if I caused you sorrow by my letter, I do not regret it." He admits he did regret it for a while, but that's not where he lands. Now he stands by it.

explanations.answer: Their sorrow led them to repentance
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "…I rejoice, not because you were made sorrowful, but because your sorrow led you to repentance." He doesn't enjoy anyone's tears, friend. The joy is in where the sorrow went. That's a good father's heart.

explanations.answer: His letter proved that he was right
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that anywhere. He says he rejoices "because your sorrow led you to repentance." His joy isn't about winning. It's about what happened in them.
The text says nothing about the church going quiet. Paul rejoices "because your sorrow led you to repentance." A quiet room isn't what he's celebrating. He's celebrating a turn of heart.
Paul says the opposite. They felt the sorrow God intended, "…and so were not harmed in any way by us." The letter stung, but it didn't hurt them. Not in any way, friend.
Right, Paul says they "were not harmed in any way by us." Sorrow happened, but harm didn't. That's the sorrow God had intended. Paul puts it plainly.
Paul says, "Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret…" Salvation, friend, and nothing to regret afterward. That's the end of the road for this kind of sorrow.

Shame isn't where Paul says godly sorrow leads. He writes, "Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret…" Without regret is a big part of it. No leftover shame to carry around.
Silence isn't the word. Paul says godly sorrow "brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret…" It leads somewhere good, and Paul names the place. It's salvation.
Paul says, "…but worldly sorrow brings death." It's a heavy line, and he doesn't soften it. He sets it next to godly sorrow, which leads to salvation. Two kinds of sorrow, two very different endings.
Peace isn't what Paul says worldly sorrow brings. He writes, "…but worldly sorrow brings death." It's a heavy line, and I think he means it to be. Godly sorrow is the one that leads to salvation.
Paul doesn't say wisdom. He says, "…but worldly sorrow brings death." Setting it beside godly sorrow, which leads to salvation, the difference is clear. One road gets you home and the other doesn't.
Paul says, "In every way you have proved yourselves to be innocent in this matter." In every way, friend. That's right after his big list of what their godly sorrow produced.
Paul says the reverse. He writes, "In every way you have proved yourselves to be innocent in this matter." I know the letter stung, but this is how he sums them up. Innocent.

Careless is nowhere in this verse. Paul looks at all that earnestness and eagerness and says, "In every way you have proved yourselves to be innocent in this matter." Careless people don't produce a list like that.

explanations.answer: So they'd see how devoted they were to him
explanations.explanation: Paul says he wrote "…that your earnestness on our behalf would be made clear to you in the sight of God." He wasn't writing to point fingers at the one who did wrong or the one who was harmed. He wanted them to see their own earnestness. I think that's a gift, friend.

explanations.answer: So they'd stop doubting that he was an apostle
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't give that reason here. He says he wrote "…that your earnestness on our behalf would be made clear to you in the sight of God." It's easy to guess a reason that sounds right. Stick with the one he states.

explanations.answer: So other churches would hear what happened
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. Paul says he wrote "…that your earnestness on our behalf would be made clear to you in the sight of God." The point was for the Corinthians themselves to see something. No news spreading is mentioned.
Paul says, "…we were even more delighted by the joy of Titus." He was encouraged already, and seeing Titus so happy topped it. His joy had a second helping. I'd take that every time.
Paul actually says, "…we were even more delighted by the joy of Titus." Titus's spirit was refreshed by all of them, and that joy rubbed off on Paul. More delighted, friend, not less.
Paul says the opposite: "Indeed, I was not embarrassed by anything I had boasted to him about you." He talked them up to Titus, and they held up. No red face at all.
Paul writes, "Indeed, I was not embarrassed by anything I had boasted to him about you." Everything he said to Titus held up. That's a relief if you've ever bragged on somebody ahead of time.

explanations.answer: All obedient with fear and trembling
explanations.explanation: Paul says Titus remembers "…you were all obedient as you welcomed him with fear and trembling." All of them, friend, not just a few. That memory made Titus's affection for them even greater.

explanations.answer: All hesitant with doubts and questions
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't describe a hesitant welcome. He says Titus remembers "…you were all obedient as you welcomed him with fear and trembling." Obedient is the word he picks. Nobody was dragging their feet at the door.

explanations.answer: All proud with boasting and praise
explanations.explanation: Pride and boasting aren't in Paul's picture here. He says Titus remembers "…you were all obedient as you welcomed him with fear and trembling." It's a humble welcome, and Titus loved them more for it.
Paul ends with, "I rejoice that I can have complete confidence in you." Complete, friend, with no gaps. After all that sorrow and repentance, it's a warm way to close.
Shaky isn't how Paul ends. He says, "I rejoice that I can have complete confidence in you." Complete confidence means nothing wobbling. After this whole passage, it fits.
Paul's confidence isn't fading. He writes, "I rejoice that I can have complete confidence in you." It's the opposite of fading, friend. It's full strength.
